strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP deployment problem: adapting LLMs while producing quantized weights without a separate high-precision adapter path. Quantizing the combined pretrained and low-rank weights is a coherent design that avoids QA-LoRA's structural restriction on adapters.

The evaluation covers several model families and sizes, both 3-bit and 4-bit quantization, seven commonsense tasks, and MMLU. Some reported improvements are substantial: on LLaMA-2 7B at 3 bits, L4Q achieves 61.3% commonsense accuracy versus 57.9% for the strongest reported quantized baseline. Initialization, rank, and group-size ablations provide additional evidence.

The paper measures practical efficiency alongside accuracy. Reported 7B training memory is 25.4 GB, close to LoRA's 25.1 GB and substantially below conventional QAT's 79.5 GB. Appendix F specifies the inference backend and reports throughput across batch sizes, supporting the practical benefit of eliminating the adapter path.
weaknesses: Baseline fidelity needs clarification. The explicitly marked uniform-quantization versions of QLoRA and LoftQ establish a narrower comparison than superiority over their published configurations. More seriously, Section 4.1 states that adapters use Kaiming initialization for A and zeros for B, leaving unclear whether LoftQ retains its defining SVD initialization. Its near-chance 3-bit MMLU results make this consequential. The manuscript should document these implementations and validate their configurations before drawing broad comparative conclusions.

The training-efficiency comparisons have material confounds. Appendix D uses sequence length 128 specifically for L4Q on the 33B model, versus 2048 elsewhere, undermining direct interpretation of the largest-model memory and timing comparisons. Total training times also compare 25K L4Q iterations with 50K iterations for PTQ-based methods; a training-loss curve on one model does not establish comparable time to a target validation quality across configurations. L4Q's substantially higher memory consumption than QLoRA—25.4 versus 7.9 GB at 7B—also deserves greater prominence.

The central backward implementation is insufficiently specified for confident reproduction. Equations (29)–(30) ambiguously apply a weight-shaped clipping condition to adapter-shaped gradients. With weight gradient G and clipping mask M, the required contractions are dA = alpha B^T(G elementwise-multiplied by M) and dB = alpha(G elementwise-multiplied by M)A^T. The mask must precede contraction. The paper also lacks an implementation link or explicit saved-tensor/recomputation schedule explaining its memory advantage over an equally optimized QAT-LoRA implementation. LoRA scaling, microbatching, and gradient accumulation are unspecified.

The experiments do not sufficiently isolate the proposed explanation for the gains. QAT-LoRA already trains quantization and adapter parameters through a shared loss, so describing it as lacking joint optimization is imprecise. Ablations that hold initialization and training schedules fixed while varying adapter placement and quantizer learning would identify the useful components. A straightforward LoRA fine-tuning followed by PTQ baseline would also directly test the claimed advantage over separating adaptation and quantization.

Several accuracy advantages are small, and no repeated-run variability or confidence intervals are reported. For example, 4-bit LLaMA-1 7B MMLU 5-shot improves from QA-LoRA's 35.6% to 35.7%. Superiority is also not universal: at 3 bits, LLaMA-2 13B MMLU 5-shot is 50.0% versus QLoRA's 50.6%. These results support a promising contribution, but the unresolved comparison and reproducibility concerns prevent a clear Findings recommendation.
